name: Tyrannosaurus rex
fact: The skull of “Sue” (FMNH PR 2081, Field Museum, Chicago) shows healed bite marks from another T. rex — direct fossil evidence they fought each other. Her thigh bone is 1.33 meters long.
know: Growth rings in the bones, like tree rings, show a teenage growth spurt of about 2 kg a day; few T. rex lived past 30. Fossil dung packed with crushed bone confirms the bone-shattering bite — the strongest of any land animal known.
debate: Was the smaller “Nanotyrannus” a separate species or a teenage T. rex? A nearly full-grown skeleton described in 2025 points to a separate species — an argument that has run for over 30 years.
discovery: First described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905 (AMNH 973). Holotype discovered in 1902 near Hell Creek Formation, Montana by Barnum Brown.
keyResearchers: Osborn, H.F. (1905), Brown, B. (1902), Horner & Lessem (1993), Hutchinson & Garcia (2002)
citation: Osborn, H.F. (1905). Tyrannosaurus and other Cretaceous carnivorous dinosaurs. Bulletin of the AMNH 21:259–265.

name: Triceratops
fact: Modern research recognized two species in Hell Creek Formation. The herding bone beds suggest they were social animals.
know: One Triceratops skull has a brow horn bitten off and a frill gouged by T. rex teeth — and the bone had healed. It fought a tyrannosaur and lived.
taxonomy: Dinosauria › Saurischia › Ornithischia › Ceratopsia › Ceratopsidae › Chasmosaurinae
discovery: First described 1889 by Othniel Charles Marsh. Later Hatcher collected 31 more skulls (1889–1891).
keyResearchers: Marsh, O.C. (1889), Hatcher, J.B. (1891), Forster, C. (1996), Scannella & Fowler (2009)
citation: Marsh, O.C. (1889). Notice of gigantic horned dinosaurs. American Journal of Science 38:173–175.

name: Ankylosaurus
fact: Brown's holotype shows the original specimen had over 30 bony armor plates. Modern analysis reveals it could swing its club tail with enough force to break bones.
discovery: Holotype AMNH 5895 discovered in 1906 by Barnum Brown in Hell Creek Formation, Montana.
keyResearchers: Brown, B. (1908), Coombs, W.P. (2004), Vickaryous et al.
citation: Brown, B. (1908). The Ankylosauridae, a new family of armored dinosaurs. Bulletin of the AMNH 24:187–201.

name: Velociraptor
fact: Not as big as Hollywood showed! But deadly smart — could hunt in groups, used that sickle claw to disembowel prey. Brain-to-body ratio of a smart bird. Probably had feathers. A nightmare for small animals.
know: A forearm bone found in Mongolia has a row of small bumps — quill knobs, where large feathers were anchored, just as in a modern turkey. The real Velociraptor was turkey-sized, too: about 15 kg.

name: Parasaurolophus
fact: Had a crazy curved horn-crest on its head! Could make loud honking sounds to communicate — the Cretaceous school bus driver! Herds migrated together like modern caribou, trumpeting to each other.

name: Mosasaurus
fact: At 18 meters, it was an ocean apex predator, ruling Cretaceous seas for millions of years.
know: A giant skull dug from a chalk mine at Maastricht in the 1770s helped Georges Cuvier convince the world that species can go extinct — an idea many then thought impossible. Mosasaurs were lizards, related to monitors and snakes, and gave birth to live young at sea.
discovery: Genus proposed 1822 by Conybeare. Mantell added species epithet hoffmannii in 1829.
keyResearchers: Conybeare, W.D. (1822), Mantell, G. (1829), Cope, E.D. (1869)
citation: Mantell, G. (1829). The Geology of the South-East of England. Longman, Rees, Orme, Brown & Green.

name: Spinosaurus
fact: That sail might have been a hump for fat storage, not a display sail. A semi-aquatic predator — 17 meters long, 7 tonnes.
know: A skeleton from Morocco described in 2020 has a tall, flexible, paddle-like tail — unlike any other dinosaur's. Its bones are dense and solid, like a penguin's or a hippo's, which helps an animal stay submerged.
debate: A swimmer that chased fish underwater, or a wader that snatched them from the shallows like a giant heron? Specialists read the same bones both ways.
discovery: Fossils discovered 1912 in Egypt, described 1915 by Ernst Stromer.
keyResearchers: Stromer, E. (1915), Bailey, J.B. (1997), Sereno et al. (2007)
citation: Stromer, E. (1915). Ergebnisse der Stromerinnen Theropoden-Expedition. Abhandlungen 28:1–79.

name: Therizinosaurus
fact: Giant hand claws up to 90 cm long! A gentle giant that used them to pull down branches. Weighed as much as an elephant but was strictly vegetarian. Evolution's craziest-looking plant-eater.

name: Archaeoceratops
c: Dinosaurs › Horned & dome-headed › Early horned dinosaurs
fact: The smallest ceratopsian — ancestor of Triceratops! Showed that horned dinosaurs started tiny. Each generation got bigger. Over 30 million years, they went from dog-sized to 8-ton tanks.

name: Iguanodon
fact: The second dinosaur ever named (1825) and the one that helped scientists realize dinosaurs were not just giant lizards. Iguanodon had a distinctive spiked thumb originally mistaken for a nose horn. It could walk on two or four legs and its teeth were among the most complex chewing systems of any dinosaur.
know: The second dinosaur ever named (1825). Its thumb spike was first reconstructed as a horn on its nose — until 1878, when coal miners in Belgium broke into a pocket holding more than thirty complete skeletons, 322 m underground.

name: Pteranodon
habitat: Shallow inland sea of North America
fact: The most famous pterosaur and the largest flying animal of its time. Despite its enormous wingspan Pteranodon weighed only about 20 kg - lighter than a large turkey. Its backward-sweeping crest likely acted as a rudder for steering in flight.

name: Quetzalcoatlus
fact: The largest flying animal ever to exist - with the wingspan of a small airplane and a height on the ground matching a modern giraffe. Quetzalcoatlus stalked inland plains like a giant heron, snatching small dinosaurs and hatchlings from the ground.
know: With a 10–11 m wingspan it was among the largest flying animals ever. Its bones show it walked on all fours with wings folded, stalking prey like a stork, and probably launched itself with a leap from its powerful arms.

name: Carnotaurus
fact: The only large theropod with bull-like horns above its eyes - possibly used for combat with rivals. It had arms even smaller than T. rex. However its legs were built for speed, and biomechanical studies suggest it may have been the fastest large predatory dinosaur ever.

name: Elasmosaurus
habitat: Western Interior Seaway of North America
fact: A plesiosaur so extreme that when Edward Drinker Cope first described it in 1868 he attached the skull to the tail end by mistake. Elasmosaurus had 72 neck vertebrae - more than any other known vertebrate. It used its snake-like neck to ambush fish from below.

name: Utahraptor
fact: The biggest “raptor” ever found: as heavy as a polar bear, with a 22-cm killing claw on each foot. It was named in 1993 — the same summer Jurassic Park filled cinemas with raptors scaled up far beyond the real Velociraptor.
know: A nine-tonne block of sandstone from Utah holds the remains of an adult, juveniles and a baby that died together, perhaps trapped in quicksand. It is still being worked on, grain by grain.

name: Baryonyx
fact: A crocodile-snouted dinosaur with a 31-cm hooked claw on each thumb, found in a Surrey clay pit in 1983 by William Walker, a plumber and amateur fossil hunter.
know: Inside its ribcage were the acid-etched scales of a large fish — the first direct proof of a fish-eating dinosaur — together with the bones of a young Iguanodon.

name: Amargasaurus
fact: A small sauropod with two rows of spines up to 60 cm tall running down its neck.
debate: Bare horns for defence, or the frame of a skin sail? A 2022 microscope study of the spine bone found the texture of bone covered by skin, favouring a sail — but not everyone is convinced.

name: Sinosauropteryx
fact: Found by a farmer in 1996, this was the first dinosaur outside the bird line discovered with feathers — a coat of simple fuzz. It changed how every dinosaur has been pictured since.
know: Fossil pigment capsules show it was chestnut-brown above and pale below, with a striped tail and a dark “bandit mask” across the eyes — camouflage for open country.

name: Yutyrannus
fact: A 1.4-tonne cousin of T. rex covered in shaggy feathers up to 20 cm long — the largest feathered animal known.
know: Three skeletons found together all show the filaments. Liaoning then had cool winters (averaging about 10 °C over the year), so a warm coat made sense even for a giant.

name: Psittacosaurus
c: Dinosaurs › Horned & dome-headed › Early horned dinosaurs
fact: An early relative of Triceratops with a parrot-like beak, known from more than 400 skeletons — from hatchlings to adults.
know: One specimen in Frankfurt preserves its skin so well that scientists have mapped its colour (dark above, light below — forest camouflage), a row of bristles on its tail, its cloaca, and even its belly button.

name: Mei long
fact: A small dinosaur preserved exactly as it fell asleep: legs folded beneath it, head tucked under one arm — the roosting posture of a modern bird.
know: It was buried so suddenly, probably by volcanic ash or gas, that it never stirred. Behaviour almost never fossilises; this is sleep, 125 million years old.

name: Confuciusornis
fact: The earliest known bird with a toothless beak. Thousands have been found, sometimes in flocks killed together by volcanic eruptions.
know: Some have a pair of long ribbon tail feathers and some do not. A spongy tissue found only in egg-laying female birds turned up in one without ribbons — so the ribbons belonged to the males.

name: Repenomamus
fact: Mammals of the dinosaur age were not all shrew-sized. This badger-sized hunter ate dinosaurs.
know: One skeleton has the chopped-up bones of a baby Psittacosaurus where its stomach was. A second fossil, described in 2023, appears to show one gripping and biting a Psittacosaurus three times its size as both were buried by a volcanic flow.

name: Microraptor
fact: A four-winged dinosaur with flight feathers on both arms and legs. It could certainly glide and may have managed powered flight — an experiment separate from the one that led to birds.
know: Its feathers held stacked, sausage-shaped pigment capsules — the arrangement that makes a crow or starling shimmer. It was glossy black. Stomach contents show it ate birds, fish, lizards and small mammals.

name: Suchomimus
fact: A fish-eater with a long, narrow, crocodile-like snout packed with over 100 teeth, and a low sail along its back. The Sahara where it was found was then a land of broad rivers.

name: Ouranosaurus
fact: A relative of Iguanodon with tall spines along its back.
debate: A thin sail for display or shedding heat — or the base of a fatty hump, like a bison's, for surviving dry seasons? The spines look more like those of humped mammals than of sail-backed reptiles.

name: Leaellynasaura
size: About 90 cm, most of it tail
means: Leaellyn's lizard — named for the discoverers' daughter
fact: A small plant-eater that lived inside the Antarctic Circle, when Australia was still joined to Antarctica. For weeks or months each winter the sun did not rise.
know: Its fossils were tunnelled out of a sea cliff with mining equipment. They show that dinosaurs lived year-round in places with long, dark, cold winters — hard to do for a cold-blooded animal.

name: Deinonychus
fact: The dinosaur that changed everything. Found in Montana in 1964, it was plainly built for speed and agility — and the “raptors” of Jurassic Park are modelled on it, not on the turkey-sized Velociraptor.
know: John Ostrom's 1969 description argued that an animal like this could not have been a sluggish, cold-blooded reptile. That started the “dinosaur renaissance” — and revived the idea, now proven, that birds are living dinosaurs.

name: Nigersaurus
fact: A sauropod with a mouth like a vacuum-cleaner head: wider than its skull, straight across the front, and lined with more than 500 teeth for cropping plants at ground level.
know: Counting growth lines in its teeth shows each one was replaced about every 14 days — the fastest known in any dinosaur. Its skull bones are so thin that light shines through them.

name: Acrocanthosaurus
fact: North America's top predator 45 million years before T. rex, with a muscular ridge along its back.
know: At Glen Rose, Texas, a trail of big three-toed footprints follows a trail of sauropod footprints across an ancient mudflat, step for step — quite possibly an Acrocanthosaurus stalking its prey.

name: Sauroposeidon
fact: Possibly the tallest animal that ever lived — able to look into a sixth-floor window. Its neck bones are 1.4 m long each, and when a dog handler found them in a prison yard in Oklahoma in 1994 they were taken for fossil tree trunks.

name: Sarcosuchus
fact: “SuperCroc”: a river predator twice as long as the largest living crocodile, with a bulbous snout. Despite the look, it belongs to an extinct side branch, not the line that led to today's crocodiles.

name: Borealopelta
fact: The best-preserved armoured dinosaur ever found — it looks like a sleeping statue, with every plate, spike and scale in place. An oil-sands excavator operator, Shawn Funk, hit it in 2011. Its carcass had drifted out to sea, sunk on its back and been sealed in mud.
know: Chemical traces of pigment show it was reddish-brown above and pale below. Only animals that are hunted need camouflage — so even a 1.3-tonne walking tank had something to fear. Its last meal, mostly ferns, is still in its stomach.

name: Muttaburrasaurus
fact: Australia's best-known dinosaur, found by a grazier mustering cattle in 1963. A hollow, bulging bony nose may have been a sound chamber for calls.

name: Patagotitan
fact: Among the largest animals ever to walk the Earth — as long as three buses, as heavy as ten elephants. A farm worker noticed the tip of a thigh bone sticking out of the ground; the bone turned out to be 2.4 m long.
know: At least six individuals died at the same spot, at three different times. Because so much of the skeleton is known, its weight can be estimated from the thickness of the leg bones rather than guessed.

name: Carcharodontosaurus
fact: A giant hunter with serrated, blade-like teeth 20 cm long, built for slicing rather than crushing. It shared North Africa's rivers with Spinosaurus.
know: The first skeleton, found in Egypt, was destroyed with Spinosaurus when Munich's museum was bombed in 1944. A new skull 1.6 m long was found in Morocco in 1995.

name: Giganotosaurus
fact: About as long as T. rex, though more lightly built and with a smaller brain. It was found in 1993 by Rubén Carolini, a car mechanic who hunted fossils in his spare time.

name: Argentinosaurus
fact: A contender for the heaviest land animal of all time. The rancher who found the first bone in 1987 thought it was a petrified log. A single backbone is taller than a person.
debate: Only about a tenth of the skeleton is known, so its size is scaled up from more complete relatives — estimates range from 60 to more than 90 tonnes.

name: Australovenator
fact: A light, fast predator with large hand claws, nicknamed “Banjo”. It was found tangled with the bones of a sauropod nicknamed “Matilda” in a dried-up waterhole — both names from Australia's bush poet, Banjo Paterson.

name: Hesperornis
fact: A flightless diving bird as long as a person, with tiny wings, huge paddling feet — and a beak full of teeth.
know: Described in the 1870s, toothed birds were exactly the “missing link” between reptiles and birds that Darwin's theory predicted. Darwin wrote to its describer, O. C. Marsh, that his work gave “the best support to the theory of evolution”.

name: Deinosuchus
fact: A giant relative of alligators that lived on both shores of the sea that split North America. It was easily big enough to eat dinosaurs.
know: Dinosaur bones and sea-turtle shells from the same rocks carry deep, round punctures that match its teeth.

name: Archelon
fact: The largest turtle that ever lived — the size of a small car. Its shell was a frame of bone covered in leathery skin, like a modern leatherback's.

name: Maiasaura
fact: At “Egg Mountain” in Montana, nests full of crushed eggshell are spaced one adult body-length apart, like a seabird colony. The babies stayed in the nest and were fed.
know: Hatchlings' leg joints were not fully formed — they could not have walked far — yet their teeth were already worn from eating. Someone was bringing them food. In 1985 a piece of Maiasaura bone and eggshell flew on the Space Shuttle: the first dinosaur in space.

name: Stenonychosaurus (Troodon)
fact: For its body size it had one of the biggest brains of any dinosaur outside the birds, plus large forward-facing eyes. Its nests show it sat on its eggs, half-buried, to keep them warm.
debate: For decades this animal was called Troodon — a name based on a single tooth found in 1856. Since 2017 many specialists consider that name too poorly founded to use.

name: Corythosaurus
fact: A duck-billed dinosaur with a hollow, plate-shaped crest. Air passages looped through it like the tubing of a horn, giving each animal a deep, resonant call.
know: The first skeleton (1912) came with large patches of fossilised skin. Two others lie on the bottom of the Atlantic: the ship carrying them to Britain was sunk by a German raider in 1916.

name: Gorgosaurus
fact: A lighter, faster cousin of T. rex that lived about ten million years earlier.
know: In 2023 a young Gorgosaurus was described with its last two meals still in its stomach: the hind legs of two baby bird-like dinosaurs. Teenage tyrannosaurs hunted small, fast prey — a different job in the ecosystem from the bone-crushing adults.

name: Centrosaurus
fact: A horned dinosaur with one long nose horn and small hooks curling from its frill. It travelled in herds of thousands.
know: Near Hilda, Alberta, at least 14 bonebeds lie in the same rock layer across 2.3 square kilometres — one enormous herd, drowned when a tropical storm flooded the coastal plain.

name: Kosmoceratops
fact: Fifteen horns and hooks — the most decorated skull of any dinosaur known: one on the nose, one over each eye, one on each cheek, and ten curling forward from the frill.
know: Its relatives in Alberta, on the same narrow island continent, were different species entirely. Something — climate, or rivers and mountains — kept northern and southern dinosaurs apart.

name: Zuul
means: Named for the monster in Ghostbusters; its species name means “destroyer of shins”
fact: An armoured dinosaur with a 3-m tail ending in a sledgehammer of bone, preserved with skin and the horny sheaths of its spikes.
know: The armour along its flanks — not its back — has broken and healed spikes. That is where another Zuul's tail club would land, not a tyrannosaur's jaws: the clubs were mainly for fighting each other.

name: Styracosaurus
fact: A 60-cm nose horn and a frill crowned with four to six long spikes. The frill was probably for show — recognising your own kind, impressing mates — more than for defence.

name: Dreadnoughtus
fact: The most complete giant titanosaur ever found: about 70% of the skeleton behind the skull. And the bones show it was still growing when it died.
debate: How heavy? The first estimate, from leg-bone thickness, was 59 tonnes. Three-dimensional body models suggest 30–40. Weighing an animal nobody has seen alive is hard.

name: Protoceratops
c: Dinosaurs › Horned & dome-headed › Early horned dinosaurs
fact: A hornless early cousin of Triceratops, so common in the Gobi that skeletons of every age from hatchling to adult are known.
know: The “Fighting Dinosaurs”, found in 1971, are a Protoceratops and a Velociraptor locked together: the raptor's claw in the plant-eater's neck, its arm clamped in the beak. A collapsing dune buried them mid-struggle.

name: Oviraptor
means: Egg thief — a name it did not deserve
fact: Found in 1923 lying on a nest of eggs and accused of stealing them. Seventy years later an embryo inside one of those eggs turned out to be a baby oviraptorid. It was not a thief; it was a parent.
know: Related skeletons have since been found sitting on nests with their feathered arms spread over the eggs — the brooding posture of a bird, in an animal that could not fly.

name: Antarctopelta
fact: The first dinosaur ever discovered in Antarctica, found in 1986 by Argentine geologists. It took ten field seasons to chip the armoured skeleton out of the frozen ground.

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
fact: Where other horned dinosaurs had a nose horn, this one had a huge, rough pad of bone. It lived as far north as Arctic Alaska, through months of winter darkness.
know: A bonebed in Alberta found by a schoolteacher in 1974 holds hundreds of animals of all ages — a herd lost together, probably in a river flood.

name: Edmontosaurus
habitat: Coastal plains from Colorado to Alaska
fact: The commonest large plant-eater in T. rex's world, with a broad bill and about a thousand teeth packed into grinding batteries.
know: Several “mummies” preserve skin over much of the body; one showed a fleshy comb on the head, like a rooster's, that left no trace in bone. A tail with a healed T. rex bite proves T. rex attacked living prey — and that this one got away.

name: Albertosaurus
fact: Found in 1884 by Joseph Tyrrell, a young geologist looking for coal — the museum at Drumheller is named for him.
know: At one site at least a dozen Albertosaurus of different ages, and probably more than twenty, died together.
debate: A pack that hunted together, or loners drawn to the same trap in a drought? The bones cannot yet tell us.

name: Tarbosaurus
fact: Asia's cousin of T. rex, nearly as large and with even smaller arms.
know: In 2012 a Tarbosaurus skeleton smuggled out of Mongolia sold at auction in New York for over a million dollars. A court case — titled United States v. One Tyrannosaurus Bataar Skeleton — sent it home, and changed how the fossil trade is policed.

name: Gallimimus
fact: Built like a giant ostrich: toothless beak, long neck, long legs, and probably the fastest dinosaur of its world. The flocking herd in Jurassic Park is Gallimimus.

name: Deinocheirus
fact: For almost 50 years this dinosaur was just a pair of arms: 2.4 m long, with huge claws, found in 1965. What kind of monster did they belong to?
know: Two skeletons found in 2006 and 2009 — plus a skull and feet taken by poachers and recovered from Europe — gave the answer in 2014: a humpbacked, duck-billed, hoofed giant that ate plants and fish. Nobody had guessed anything like it.

name: Saltasaurus
fact: The first sauropod found with armour: its back was studded with bony plates and pea-sized nodules. Until then, armour plates found near sauropod bones had been assigned to other dinosaurs.
know: At Auca Mahuevo in Patagonia, related titanosaurs left thousands of eggs across a floodplain. Some hold embryos with fossilised skin — tiny scales, already armoured.

name: Pachycephalosaurus
fact: Its skull roof was a dome of solid bone up to 25 cm thick, ringed with knobs and spikes.
know: About one dome in five has healed wounds on top — what you would expect if they butted heads. And two “other” spiky-headed species, including one named Dracorex hogwartsia, are probably just Pachycephalosaurus teenagers: the dome grew and the spikes shrank with age.

name: Majungasaurus
fact: The top predator of Madagascar, with a short, deep skull and a single domed horn. Madagascar was already an island, and its dinosaurs evolved in isolation.
know: Majungasaurus bones carry tooth marks that match only one animal there: Majungasaurus. It is the clearest evidence of cannibalism in any dinosaur.

name: Alamosaurus
means: Ojo Alamo lizard — named for a spring in New Mexico, not the fort
fact: The largest dinosaur known from North America, and one of the last sauropods anywhere — it was alive when the asteroid struck.
know: For about 30 million years before it, North American rocks contain no sauropods at all. Alamosaurus's closest relatives are South American, so its ancestors probably walked north when the two continents drew close.

name: Rajasaurus
fact: A stocky, single-horned predator from India — then an island continent drifting north across the ocean, alone, at up to 15–20 cm a year.
know: Its bones lie in sediments sandwiched between flows of the Deccan Traps: Rajasaurus lived and hunted while one of the largest volcanic outpourings in Earth's history was under way around it.

name: Asteriornis
means: Asteria's bird — after a goddess of falling stars who turned into a quail
fact: The “Wonderchicken”: the oldest known skull of a modern-type bird, part chicken-like and part duck-like. It lived less than a million years before the asteroid.
know: The skull was hidden inside a fist-sized rock that showed only some broken leg bones. A CT scan in 2018 revealed it, complete, staring back from the screen. Small, ground-living, seashore birds like this were the kind of dinosaur that survived.

name: Hatzegopteryx
habitat: A large island in the European archipelago
fact: A giraffe-sized pterosaur with a short, immensely strong neck. On Hațeg Island the dinosaurs had shrunk — the local sauropod was the size of a pony — and no big meat-eating dinosaur lived there. The top predator walked on its wings.

name: Mapusaurus
fact: A giant related to Giganotosaurus. At least seven individuals of different sizes were found together, hinting that they lived — or at least died — in groups.

name: Concavenator
fact: A meat-eater with a strange, pointed hump on its back. Bumps on its forearm look like the anchor points for quills.
debate: Quill knobs, or just muscle attachments? It matters: true quills would mean feather-like structures far from the bird line.

name: Irritator
fact: A spinosaur named out of frustration: dealers had sculpted plaster onto the skull to make it look more complete, and scientists had to remove it.

name: Sinornithosaurus
fact: A feathered raptor with grooved teeth.
debate: Venomous? A study published at the end of 2009 said the grooves carried venom; later work found the teeth had simply shifted in their sockets. Most now doubt it.

name: Dakotaraptor
fact: A big raptor that lived alongside T. rex in the last days of the dinosaurs. Bumps on its forearm anchored large wing feathers.

name: Halszkaraptor
habitat: Rivers and lakes in a desert
fact: A raptor with a swan-like neck and duck-like snout — possibly a swimmer that caught fish.
know: The skeleton was poached, sold abroad and bought by a collector, then returned to Mongolia. Scientists scanned it with a particle-accelerator X-ray beam to prove it was genuine.

name: Citipati
fact: The famous “Big Mama”: a skeleton sitting on its nest with arms spread around the eggs, just like a brooding bird.

name: Anzu
fact: Nicknamed the “chicken from hell”: a tall crest, a toothless beak and long legs, in T. rex's world.

name: Daspletosaurus
fact: A heavy tyrannosaur from just before T. rex. Its face was covered in thick, sensitive scales — like a crocodile's.

name: Lythronax
fact: A tyrannosaur with a wide back to its skull and forward-facing eyes — features once thought to belong only to T. rex, 14 million years later.

name: Qianzhousaurus
fact: Nicknamed “Pinocchio rex” for its long, narrow snout. It shows tyrannosaurs came in more shapes than once thought.

name: Nanuqsaurus
fact: A tyrannosaur from far inside the Arctic Circle, where winters were dark for months.

name: Struthiomimus
fact: An “ostrich mimic” built for speed, with a toothless beak and long legs.

name: Ornithomimus
fact: Adult skeletons from Alberta preserve feathers on the arms in a wing-like pattern, while the young had only fuzz — wings came first for display, not flight.

name: Nothronychus
fact: A pot-bellied, long-clawed plant-eater from a meat-eating family. It was the first therizinosaur found outside Asia.

name: Masiakasaurus
fact: A small hunter whose front teeth stuck straight forward, perhaps for spearing fish. Its species is named after Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits.

name: Skorpiovenator
fact: An abelisaur with a deeply wrinkled skull — named “scorpion hunter” because the dig site swarmed with scorpions.

name: Rapetosaurus
fact: A Madagascar titanosaur. A baby that died within weeks of hatching already had proportions like an adult's — newborns had to fend for themselves.

name: Paralititan
fact: A giant titanosaur that lived in mangrove swamps on the coast of what is now the Sahara.

name: Futalognkosaurus
fact: One of the most complete giant titanosaurs, found with fossil fish and leaves — a snapshot of its whole world.

name: Bajadasaurus
fact: A sauropod with long spines on its neck curving forward over its head — probably a defence, or for display.

name: Euoplocephalus
fact: Even its eyelids were armoured. A swing of its bony tail club could break a predator's leg.

name: Edmontonia
fact: An armoured dinosaur with long spikes pointing forward from its shoulders — perhaps for shoving rivals.

name: Sauropelta
fact: A nodosaur with tall spikes along its neck. It shared its world with Deinonychus.

name: Gastonia
fact: A spiky ankylosaur found in the same Utah quarry as Utahraptor — perhaps one of its prey.

name: Minmi
habitat: Coastal plains by an inland sea
fact: Named after a road crossing in Queensland, and one of the first armoured dinosaurs found in the Southern Hemisphere. A close relative, Kunbarrasaurus, was found with its last meal of seeds, fruit and chewed leaves still inside.

name: Pinacosaurus
fact: Groups of young Pinacosaurus died together, buried side by side, probably in a sandstorm — evidence the youngsters stuck together.

name: Lambeosaurus
fact: A duck-bill with a hatchet-shaped hollow crest. Air passages inside made it a natural trumpet.

name: Hypacrosaurus
fact: Nests with eggs and embryos in Montana show how babies grew. Cartilage cells, and possibly traces of DNA chemistry, were reported inside one embryo's skull in 2020.

name: Shantungosaurus
fact: The biggest duck-billed dinosaur — as long as a bus and as heavy as two elephants, but still able to walk on two legs.

name: Saurolophus
fact: A duck-bill with a spike-like crest pointing backwards — found both in Alberta and in Mongolia, so it crossed between the continents.

name: Olorotitan
fact: Its name means “giant swan”: a long-necked duck-bill with a fan-shaped crest, from Russia's Far East.

name: Brachylophosaurus
fact: “Leonardo”, found in 2000, is a mummy: skin, muscle and stomach contents of conifer needles, ferns and pollen were all preserved.

name: Tethyshadros
fact: A dwarf duck-bill that lived on islands where Italy is now. The skeleton nicknamed “Antonio” is one of the most complete dinosaurs from Europe.

name: Tenontosaurus
fact: A long-tailed plant-eater often found surrounded by Deinonychus teeth — the evidence that started the idea of pack-hunting raptors.

name: Hypsilophodon
fact: A small, fast plant-eater. For decades it was drawn sitting in trees — a mistake corrected in the 1970s. It was a ground runner.

name: Thescelosaurus
fact: One of the last dinosaurs. A skeleton nicknamed “Willo” was claimed in 2000 to have a fossil heart.
debate: The “heart” was later shown to be an ironstone lump that formed after death. Soft organs almost never fossilise.

name: Chasmosaurus
fact: Its huge frill was mostly holes — big windows of bone covered by skin. Light, and made for showing off rather than defence.

name: Einiosaurus
fact: Its nose horn curved down and forward like a bottle-opener. Bonebeds suggest herds died together in droughts.

name: Torosaurus
fact: Its skull, nearly 2.8 m long, is one of the largest of any land animal.
debate: In 2010 some argued Torosaurus was just a fully grown Triceratops. Most later studies found the two were separate.

name: Nasutoceratops
fact: A big nose and long, curving brow horns like a bull's.

name: Sinoceratops
fact: The first big horned dinosaur found in Asia, in 2010. Until then, the group seemed to be only North American.

name: Leptoceratops
c: Dinosaurs › Horned & dome-headed › Early horned dinosaurs
fact: A small, hornless horned dinosaur that survived to the end of the age, beside its giant cousin Triceratops.

name: Zuniceratops
c: Dinosaurs › Horned & dome-headed › Early horned dinosaurs
fact: The earliest horned dinosaur with brow horns in North America. It was discovered in 1996 by an eight-year-old, Christopher Wolfe.

name: Regaliceratops
fact: Nicknamed “Hellboy”: its frill is edged with big plates like a crown, and its brow horns are tiny stubs.

name: Stegoceras
fact: A small dome-headed plant-eater. Computer models show its dome could take head-to-head impacts.

name: Prenocephale
fact: A dome-head from Mongolia with a rounded skull ringed by small knobs.

name: Kronosaurus
fact: A pliosaur with a skull over 2 m long. A famous Harvard skeleton was mounted too long — with extra backbones added — making it look like a 13-m monster.

name: Tylosaurus
fact: A giant mosasaur with a bony snout for ramming prey. Stomach contents include fish, sharks, a plesiosaur and even a flightless bird.

name: Xiphactinus
fact: A fanged bony fish. One famous fossil holds a 1.8-m fish, swallowed whole — the predator died, probably because its meal was too big.

name: Cretoxyrhina
fact: The “Ginsu shark”: a fast, powerful hunter shaped like a great white, with smooth blade-like teeth.

name: Tupandactylus
fact: Its head crest was taller than its whole skull — a huge sail of skin and bone, probably brightly coloured for display.

name: Pterodaustro
fact: A pterosaur with about a thousand bristle-like teeth for straining tiny animals from water, like a flamingo. It may even have been pink for the same reason.

name: Nyctosaurus
fact: A pterosaur with an antler-like crest twice as long as its skull — and no claws on its wings at all.

name: Ichthyornis
fact: A seabird with teeth and a strong flying wing. Its skull, scanned in 2018, showed a bird beak beginning to form at the jaw tip.

name: Vegavis
fact: A diving bird from Antarctica — one of the first modern-type birds. It preserves the oldest known syrinx, the organ birds use to sing and call.

name: Didelphodon
fact: A badger-sized relative of opossums with a crushing bite strong enough for snails, crabs and small dinosaurs.

name: Kaprosuchus
fact: “BoarCroc”: a crocodile relative with three sets of tusks and eyes facing forward — it hunted on land.

name: Simosuchus
fact: A pug-nosed crocodile relative with leaf-shaped teeth — it ate plants.

name: Ammonites
size: From 1 cm to over 2 m across
fact: Coiled-shell relatives of squid and octopus that lived for over 340 million years — and vanished with the dinosaurs. The biggest, Parapuzosia, had a shell nearly 2 m across.

name: Eomaia
fact: “Dawn mother”: a climbing, shrew-sized animal preserved with its fur. It is one of the earliest known relatives of placental mammals — the group that includes us.

name: Steropodon
fact: An early relative of the platypus, known from a jaw that turned to opal. It lived in Australia when Australia lay close to the South Pole.

name: Adalatherium
fact: “Crazy beast”: a badger-sized mammal from Madagascar with more holes in its snout than any known mammal, and back teeth unlike anything else. Islands breed oddities.

name: Vintana
fact: A groundhog-like plant-eater with huge eyes and a keen sense of smell — a giant among the mammals of the dinosaur age.

name: Mononykus
fact: A feathered runner with tiny, powerful arms, each ending in one big claw — probably for ripping open termite nests.

name: Shuvuuia
fact: A night hunter. Its eye bones and inner ear match those of a barn owl: it hunted in the dark by sight and sound, then dug out its prey with single-clawed arms.

name: Caudipteryx
fact: A peacock-sized dinosaur with a fan of feathers on its tail and feathered arms too short to fly. It swallowed stones to grind its food, as chickens do.

name: Gigantoraptor
fact: A beaked, bird-like dinosaur the size of a tyrannosaur. Most of its relatives were the size of a turkey or an emu.

name: Falcarius
fact: An early therizinosaur caught in the middle of a change: a meat-eater’s body with the leaf-shaped teeth of a plant-eater.

name: Megaraptor
fact: A long-armed hunter with a 35 cm claw on its hand. The claw was first thought to belong on the foot, like a giant Velociraptor’s — hence the name.
debate: Where megaraptors sit on the dinosaur tree is unsettled: relatives of Allosaurus, or of the tyrannosaurs.

name: Austroraptor
fact: One of the biggest raptors, from Patagonia, with short arms and a long, low snout full of cone-shaped teeth — more like a fish-catcher than a Velociraptor.

name: Sinovenator
fact: A chicken-sized early troodontid with features of raptors and of the first birds mixed together — what you would expect near the point where those branches split.

name: Polacanthus
fact: An armoured dinosaur from the Isle of Wight with spikes along its sides and a solid shield of bone fused over its hips.
debate: Whether it belongs with the nodosaurs, the club-tails, or a small group of its own is still argued.

name: Mantellisaurus
fact: A lighter cousin of Iguanodon, named after Gideon Mantell. Skeletons of both were found in the Bernissart coal mine.

name: Europelta
fact: The oldest known nodosaur in Europe, found in a coal mine in Spain with two nearly complete skeletons.

name: Struthiosaurus
fact: The smallest armoured dinosaur known — about the size of a large dog. Like other animals on Europe’s islands, it had shrunk.

name: Ampelosaurus
fact: A titanosaur with bony plates and spikes set in its skin, found among the vineyards of southern France — its name means “vineyard lizard”.

name: Zalmoxes
fact: A small plant-eater of the island of Hațeg, which lay in a sea where Romania is now. Its mainland relatives were bigger.

name: Isisaurus
fact: An odd titanosaur with long front legs and a short, upright neck, a little like a giant hyena in outline. It lived in India while the Deccan volcanoes were erupting.

name: Sanajeh
fact: A snake caught in the act: its skeleton was found coiled around a crushed dinosaur egg, next to a hatchling sauropod half a metre long.

name: Balaur
fact: A stocky island animal with two big sickle claws on each foot instead of one.
debate: Named as a raptor, it may really be a large flightless bird. Either way, living on an island had made it strange.

name: Magyarosaurus
fact: A dwarf titanosaur — a tenth the weight of its mainland cousins. On an island with little food, small was better.
know: Slices of its bones under a microscope show the small skeletons are fully grown adults, not youngsters.

name: Neovenator
fact: The top hunter of what is now the Isle of Wight. Channels in its snout bones carried nerves, giving it a sensitive face like a crocodile’s.

name: Pelecanimimus
fact: An early ostrich-mimic with about 220 tiny teeth — more than any other meat-eating dinosaur — and the print of a throat pouch like a pelican’s.

name: Diamantinasaurus
fact: A stocky titanosaur from outback Queensland, nicknamed “Matilda”. It was found beside the meat-eater Australovenator; both may have died stuck in the same billabong.

name: Koolasuchus
fact: The last of the giant amphibians, alive 50 million years after its kind had died out everywhere else. It hung on in rivers near the South Pole that were too cold for crocodiles.

name: Sibirotitan
fact: A long-neck from Siberia, one of the oldest of the titanosaur line known from Asia.
